analysis.title: US EQUITIES - AI confidence is fading
key_insights: The desk says client sentiment on AI is about as negative as it has been in quite some time. The pessimism now shows up in positioning and valuations.
Prime brokerage data shows Tech was the most net sold sector globally again last week. The US Info Tech long/short ratio fell to its lowest level in the dataset, which goes back to 2016.
The mix of flow changed last week. Earlier selling was long liquidation and de-grossing, and last week saw a more pronounced pickup in new shorts.

The cash desk saw persistent NVDA supply from long-only clients. The money rotated into hyperscalers and other large-cap tech. NDX snapped a four-week losing streak, helped by semis, but appetite to re-engage still looks limited.
CTA positioning in NDX is back near max short. With positioning this light, the desk says it probably doesn't take much positive news to spark a squeeze higher.

Semis have underperformed the S&P by more than 30 percentage points since June, the sharpest relative drawdown since 2002 but short of the 1990s extremes. GS Research argues much of the move has gone too far, with some stocks discounting close to zero earnings growth in 2028.

The GS AI Semis basket trades at 11x 2028 earnings against nearly 16x for the S&P, while consensus expects 31% earnings growth in 2028. At the S&P multiple, current prices would imply 2028 earnings falling about 6%. So either the selloff went too far or investors are pricing in estimate cuts.

Investors raise two concerns. One is who pays for the additional hundreds of billions of dollars of AI spending. The other is whether enough data centers can be built, a worry that grew after the elections because of questions about limits on new construction in states like Texas.

GS Research says that even in a bearish case, new data center capacity coming online in 2028 should be roughly in line with 2027 because so much construction is underway. If additional projects proceed, the 2028 figure could be more than 50% higher. The open question is how much growth slows, not whether the buildout stops.

Financing is the bigger worry. AI companies want to spend more than the cash they generate, so they must borrow or bring in outside investors. Borrowing is getting more expensive and credit market costs are rising. GIR thinks existing NVDA commitments should hold but new deals of the same size may be harder to put together.
Next week's NVDA earnings and an equity capital markets event are named as possible tests of what brings investors back. NVDA is down 30% and has fallen six weeks in a row.

The 2027 Markets Outlook expects AI spending to keep growing but the pace of growth could peak early next year. AI has driven corporate earnings and equity gains more than the broader economy, so a spending slowdown could hurt stocks more than GDP.

The desk's stance is that equities can grind higher after the positioning reset, but it prefers to be more selective. It would use weakness in parts of AI to add rather than chase rallies, expects more rotation beyond infrastructure next year, and would stay disciplined on hedges.
